data.title: Rapamycin-mediated lifespan increase in mice is dose and sex dependent and metabolically distinct from dietary restriction
data.authors: Miller RA; Strong R et al.

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Rapamycin's lifespan extension in mice is dose-dependent and greater in females.
data.abstract_excerpt: Rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR kinase, increased median lifespan of genetically heterogeneous mice by 23% (males) to 26% (females) when tested at a dose threefold higher than that used in our previous studies; maximal longevity was also increased in both sexes. Rapamycin increased lifespan more in females than in males at each dose evaluated, perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels of this drug.

extracted_findings.effect: Rapamycin extends lifespan 23-26% in a dose- and sex-dependent way, metabolically distinct from dietary restriction
extracted_findings.dose: Rapamycin in food at 4.7, 14, or 42 ppm, administered from 9 months of age until death.
extracted_findings.sample_size: Pooled data from 3 sites: 300 control males, 156 males per rapamycin dose group; 280 control females, 136 females per rapamycin dose group.
extracted_findings.effect_size: Highest dose (42 ppm) increased median lifespan by 23% in males (P<0.0001) and 26% in females (P<0.0001); all three doses extended lifespan in females, and the two highest doses extended lifespan in males.
extracted_findings.limitations: Lower statistical power for site-independent analyses; Gompertz parameter estimates should be interpreted with caution due to small data sets, low statistical power, and no adjustment for site-to-site variation; increased fighting (11-22% cages removed) in highest dose male group with unknown cause.
